title: Transaction Boundaries
description: Place START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and savepoints around coherent business actions, with MySQL autocommit and failure examples.

questions.question_text: What marks the start of an explicit transaction?
questions.explanation: START TRANSACTION/BEGIN explicitly opens a transaction boundary.

questions.question_text: What are the two ways a transaction boundary can successfully or unsuccessfully close?
questions.explanation: COMMIT finalizes the transaction; ROLLBACK undoes it — the two ways to close a boundary.

questions.question_text: With MySQL autocommit enabled, no explicit transaction active, and successful standalone InnoDB DML statements, what boundary normally applies?
options: No transaction boundary exists at all
Each successful standalone statement completes its own transaction
All statements share one boundary for the entire session
questions.explanation: This statement is scoped to transactional DML outside an explicit transaction, not every possible SQL command.

questions.question_text: What operational risk can an unresolved transaction create while its connection remains active?
options: No risk — it closes automatically after a few seconds
It can retain locks or snapshots and block or burden other work
The database automatically deletes the affected rows
questions.explanation: An unresolved transaction can persist until explicitly ended or terminated by connection or system policy; do not assume an automatic short timeout.

questions.question_text: Can an ordinary MySQL CREATE TABLE inside an explicit transaction introduce an implicit commit boundary?
options: No, only explicit COMMIT/ROLLBACK can end a transaction
Yes, this statement can implicitly commit rather than remain ordinary reversible DML
DDL statements cannot be executed inside any transaction
This only happens with SELECT statements
questions.explanation: MySQL documents implicit commits for many DDL statements; other engines and special statements differ.

questions.question_text: Does starting a new transaction while one is already open behave identically across all SQL dialects?
options: No — some dialects implicitly commit the first transaction rather than truly nesting, a dialect-dependent behavior
This always raises a hard error everywhere
Nested START TRANSACTION is illegal syntax everywhere
questions.explanation: True nested transactions are not universally supported — behavior varies by dialect (see 22.13).

questions.question_text: Which operations can be treated as one supported transaction unit?
options: Only the first statement after START TRANSACTION
Participating transactional work after the start and before the actual end, provided no intervening implicit boundary occurs
Nothing — boundaries are purely conceptual with no real statements inside them
questions.explanation: The actual server boundary matters. Implicit commits, nontransactional resources, and external effects cannot be ignored merely because explicit keywords surround them.

questions.question_text: Why might an interactive database session be especially prone to leaving a transaction boundary open by mistake?
options: A person might run START TRANSACTION, get interrupted, and never issue the closing COMMIT/ROLLBACK
Interactive sessions always auto-close transactions after each command
This risk only applies to automated scripts, not interactive use
questions.explanation: Human interruption during an interactive session is a realistic, common way for a transaction to be left open.

questions.question_text: Which operations belong inside a conserving transfer transaction?
options: Both debit and credit with required checks
questions.explanation: Both balance changes form the business unit whose invariant must be protected.

questions.question_text: With MySQL autocommit enabled and no explicit transaction, two successful UPDATE statements normally form how many transactions?
questions.explanation: Each successful statement is its own transaction outside an explicit transaction.

questions.question_text: Why must pooled transaction statements use the same physical connection?
options: Transaction state belongs to the session
Rows belong to the first connection
questions.explanation: An explicit transaction is connection scoped.

questions.question_text: What does RELEASE SAVEPOINT do?
questions.explanation: Releasing a savepoint manages markers, not durability.

questions.question_text: A debit succeeds but the receiver update affects zero rows. What is the correct branch?
questions.explanation: Both updates must satisfy the operation contract.

questions.question_text: Why keep DDL outside an ordinary MySQL transfer transaction?
options: Many DDL statements cause implicit commits
DDL always runs as a nested transaction
questions.explanation: Implicit commit boundaries can defeat the expected all or nothing unit.

questions.question_text: Does one SQL statement error always roll back the entire InnoDB transaction?
options: No, rollback scope depends on the error and settings
questions.explanation: The application must handle the documented rollback scope and terminate failed work appropriately.

questions.question_text: A COMMIT acknowledgment is lost. What can the client conclude immediately?
options: Repeating it can never duplicate it
questions.explanation: The server may have committed before the network acknowledgment was lost.

questions.question_text: What does a savepoint represent?
options: An internal rollback position in one transaction
questions.explanation: Savepoints enable partial rollback inside the current transaction.

questions.question_text: After update A, savepoint S, update B, rollback to S, then full rollback, what survives?
questions.explanation: The final full rollback removes all transaction changes including A.

questions.question_text: Why avoid user interaction while a transaction holds locks?
options: It can prolong blocking and resource use
It guarantees a deadlock every time
questions.explanation: Human response time can make transactions unnecessarily long.

questions.question_text: Which design helps reconcile a retried transfer after an uncertain commit?
options: A new random transfer on every retry
A unique business operation identifier and outcome lookup
questions.explanation: A durable identity supports deduplication and discovery of an earlier result.

notes:
## What a boundary controls

A transaction boundary decides which database operations succeed together and which operations can be undone together. Imagine transferring ten credits between two campus accounts. Debiting the sender and crediting the receiver belong to one business action. If they run as separate committed statements, a failure between them leaves money missing. An explicit transaction groups them so the application can commit both changes after checking the required conditions or roll both back when the action cannot complete.

Starting a transaction does not make an arbitrary sequence correct. The application still needs valid amounts, existing accounts, authorization, sufficient funds, and protection against competing changes. Boundaries define the unit of atomicity; constraints and concurrency control determine whether that unit preserves the business invariant. In the transfer example, the invariant is that the combined balance stays constant and neither account becomes negative. State that invariant before deciding where transaction code belongs.

## Understand autocommit

MySQL normally uses autocommit mode, in which each successful statement against transactional tables forms its own transaction unless an explicit transaction is active. START TRANSACTION begins a transaction that ends at COMMIT or ROLLBACK. With autocommit disabled, work continues in transactions until the session commits or rolls back. These settings are connection state, so code using a connection pool must manage them carefully and restore the expected state before returning the connection.

Do not describe autocommit as a guarantee that every SQL statement can be undone. Storage engines and statement categories matter. These examples assume MySQL InnoDB tables. Changes to a nontransactional table cannot acquire rollback support merely because START TRANSACTION appears above them. An application that mixes transactional and nontransactional resources must explicitly analyze partial failure. Database transactions also do not automatically undo an email, a file upload, or a payment request sent to an external system.

## A transfer with an explicit decision

Use a disposable learning database for the following sequence. First create and populate the table outside the transaction. Account 1 begins at 50 credits and account 2 at 20. The application must execute the transaction statements using the same physical connection, because transactions are session scoped. Sending each statement through an unrelated pool connection does not create one transaction even when the SQL text looks like a single logical script.

```sql
CREATE TABLE credit_account (
  account_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  balance DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO credit_account VALUES (1, 50.00), (2, 20.00);

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE credit_account
SET balance = balance - 10.00
WHERE account_id = 1 AND balance >= 10.00;
-- Application: require exactly one affected row, otherwise ROLLBACK.
UPDATE credit_account
SET balance = balance + 10.00
WHERE account_id = 2;
-- Application: require exactly one affected row, otherwise ROLLBACK.
COMMIT;

SELECT account_id, balance FROM credit_account ORDER BY account_id;
```

After the successful branch, the ordered output is account 1 with 40.00 and account 2 with 30.00. The total remains 70.00. The comments describe application decisions; they are not executable conditional control flow. A script that ignores them and always commits is incomplete. If the receiver does not exist, the application must roll back the successful debit. Replacing the final COMMIT with ROLLBACK in a fresh fixture leaves the initial 50.00 and 20.00 balances unchanged.

## Savepoints are internal markers

A savepoint records a position inside an active transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT can undo work after that marker while retaining earlier work. RELEASE SAVEPOINT removes the marker; it does not commit anything. A later full rollback still undoes the retained work. Savepoints are useful when an optional operation may fail but a carefully defined larger action can still succeed. They are not independent nested transactions with separately durable inner commits.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE credit_account SET balance = balance + 2.00 WHERE account_id = 1;
SAVEPOINT optional_bonus;
UPDATE credit_account SET balance = balance + 5.00 WHERE account_id = 2;
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT optional_bonus;
COMMIT;
```

Run this on the original 50.00 and 20.00 fixture. The final balances are 52.00 and 20.00 because the second update occurs after the savepoint. This is a separate bonus example rather than a conserving transfer. Choosing a savepoint requires a business explanation: retaining only the debit of a transfer would violate the invariant even though SQL can technically express that boundary.

## Hidden boundaries and errors

In MySQL, many data definition statements cause implicit commits. Do not place CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE inside a transaction and assume a later rollback undoes the whole script. Temporary table operations have additional exceptions, so verify the specific statement category rather than applying a blanket rule. START TRANSACTION itself is not a way to nest a second transaction. Keep schema changes separate from ordinary multirow business operations and consult the documented implicit commit list when designing administrative scripts.

Error handling is equally important. A statement error does not universally imply that the entire transaction has been rolled back. InnoDB deadlocks and lock wait timeouts can have different rollback effects, influenced by the relevant configuration. Application code should catch failures, explicitly terminate the transaction as appropriate, and avoid continuing with an uncertain partial sequence. Retry policies must restart the intended business unit and distinguish retryable concurrency failures from invalid input or permanent constraint violations.

## Place the boundary in the application

Keep a transaction short enough to release locks promptly, but large enough to protect one coherent decision. Do not hold database locks while waiting for a user to answer a dialog or while a slow network request completes. Gather input first, then begin the transaction, verify conditions, modify rows, and finish. If several accounts are locked, acquire them in a consistent order across code paths to reduce deadlock opportunities. Short transactions still require retries because deadlocks can remain possible.

A lost connection during COMMIT creates an uncertain outcome for the client. The server may have committed even when the acknowledgment never arrived. Blindly repeating a transfer can apply it twice. A business operation identifier with a trusted uniqueness constraint can support idempotent processing and outcome lookup. This is an application design pattern, not a promise supplied by ROLLBACK after the connection is already gone. Plan how a caller discovers the recorded outcome before implementing automatic retries.

For external effects, one common design records the database change and an event to deliver within the same transaction. A separate worker sends the event and records delivery progress using suitable deduplication. This reduces the gap between committed data and an external notification, but still requires careful handling of repeated delivery. A transaction boundary should be described in terms of the resources it actually controls, rather than extending its guarantees to every action in the request handler.

## Exercises with decisions and results

Exercise one: the sender debit affects one row, but the receiver credit affects zero rows. What should happen? Roll back the transaction, report that the transfer did not complete, and investigate the invalid receiver. Committing would turn a validation failure into lost credits. Checking only whether SQL returned without a syntax error is insufficient; the affected row count is part of this operation's contract.

Exercise two: a transaction updates A, creates savepoint S, updates B, rolls back to S, and then fully rolls back. Which updates survive? Neither survives. Rolling back to S retained A only within the still active transaction. The full rollback removes that retained change. Releasing S instead would also leave the transaction uncommitted; marker management never replaces the final commit decision.

Exercise three: a request emails a receipt and then tries COMMIT, which fails with a connection loss. Can ROLLBACK retract the email? No. The external effect is outside the database boundary, and the database outcome may require reconciliation. Record durable operation identity and delivery intent before emitting irreversible effects. Review [atomicity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/atomicity) for all or nothing changes and [durability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/durability) for what a completed commit promises after failures.


An effective boundary review also follows every early return in the application. Validation failure, cancellation, timeout, and an unexpected exception must each leave the connection in a known state. Test the successful path and deliberately fail the second database operation to confirm that the first change disappears. Run that test against transactional tables in an isolated environment. Observing a final balance after a successful commit alone says nothing about whether the application's failure branch actually rolls back partial work.
